summary:
Penang stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' and acts of 'gross indecency', carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. The offences are not confined to Malaysian citizens, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor is exposed to them in Penang as elsewhere in the country.

State Sharia enactments criminalise same-sex intimacy and cross-dressing for Muslims only. A non-Muslim visitor is not subject to the cross-dressing offences, which carry up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and there is no law prohibiting discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage.

Enforcement since the 2018 general election has been raid-based and public. An October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced at least 20 LGBT arrests, an August raid on an LGBT venue detained twenty men, a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned, and in November 2023 Johor state authorities announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. These cases sit in other states; they establish the national enforcement climate a visitor enters in Penang.

Penang itself has appeared in the raid pattern. Days after police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur on 28 November 2025, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022, officers raided another sauna in Penang. In the Kuala Lumpur operation media were pre-tipped, detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, more than 130 people were held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened, and a magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, and transgender people are particularly vulnerable. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the practical exposure in Penang is the federal Penal Code rather than Sharia law. The documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops, and enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon, but the 2025 sauna operations show that venues and queues carry acute risk.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 for the August 2022 report 'I Don't Want to Change Myself'. Penang is among the states where interviewees lived, but the report documents national-level patterns and records no Penang-specific enforcement case.

The same report documents government-run 'rehabilitation' programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended as of June 2021, alongside conversion practices, discrimination and violence. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, and LGBT events and media content are censored.

Litigation has narrowed the state Sharia layer without loosening the federal one: the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. The federalism rulings do not touch sections 377A and 377B.

In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue a trans entrepreneur for 'insulting Islam' before she fled the country and received UNHCR protection. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his full licence to carry out enforcement actions against transgender persons.
localsOnly:
Malaysian residents who are Muslim are subject to both layers. Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, passed since the 1980s; three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments.

Residents who are Muslim also face government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats, which had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and in November 2023 Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. Federal anti-discrimination protection does not exist, and there is no legal gender-recognition procedure.

Domestic advocacy infrastructure exists. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid during the November–December 2025 sauna raids, and a constitutional challenge to the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014. The High Court had denied a request to declare that prohibition unconstitutional.

Residents are exposed to the same Penal Code provisions as visitors, and trans residents face documented lethal violence: three trans women were killed in the country in the two months before 25 June 2019, when a transgender woman was killed in Klang.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Penang-specific enforcement case appears in the Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters material; Penang is named only as a place where interviewees lived. The Penang sauna raid in late 2025 is recorded in the source inventory without a date, arrest count or charging outcome, so its scale and result remain unresolved.

Whether Penang's own Sharia enactment has been used against a trans person in the past five years is not sourced here. The inventory confirms only that all 13 states maintain such enactments and that state religious departments enforce them.

The fate of the late-2014 constitutional challenge, and whether any subsequent challenge to sections 377A and 377B has been filed, are not resolved by these sources. The Home Minister's 2 December 2025 remark about revisiting the provisions has no recorded follow-up.

Visa, immigration screening and border-procedure questions for transgender travellers are not addressed by any source in this inventory.
